extracted.intended_audience: DHS/USCIS officers, immigration attorneys, advocates, and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance for determining whether a noncitizen is likely at any time to become a 'public charge' under INA 212(a)(4), specifying which factors must be considered, how evidence (including medical reports and empirical guidance) should be used, and requirements for written decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory minimum factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers are required to consider, at a minimum, the noncitizen's age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills when determining likelihood of becoming a public charge under section 212(a)(4) of the INA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS may not alter or dismiss these statutorily mandated factors. They must be considered in every case as part of the totality-of-the-circumstances assessment; the statute does not assign preset positive/negative weights or required supporting evidence for each factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support (section 213A) — special role
rubrics_metrics.description: Where required, the sufficiency of an Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA is considered along with the statutory factors; lack of a sufficient affidavit can be outcome-determinative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule treats the absence of a required sufficient affidavit as the only single factor that may be the sole criterion for a finding. Officers must still consider it in the totality of circumstances, but its insufficiency may alone support inadmissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Public charge determinations must be based on the totality of the individual's circumstances rather than any single factor (other than a lack of a required Affidavit of Support).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS retains the longstanding 1999 Interim Field Guidance approach instead of codifying required initial evidence per factor. This reduces burdensome evidentiary requirements and promotes fair, case-specific weighting; DHS may periodically issue guidance to inform officers' assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of public cash assistance (recency, duration, amount)
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers should consider past or current receipt of public cash assistance for income maintenance, including the recency, duration, and proportion of income that assistance represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothetical examples illustrate different outcomes depending on whether assistance was a small, short-lived portion of income several years ago (may favor admissibility) versus extended, ongoing receipt with little other income (may favor inadmissibility). Officers must weigh these facts in context with other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age as a factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Age is a mandatory statutory factor to consider in assessing likelihood of becoming a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Age alone is not outcome-determinative; officers must avoid age-discriminatory conclusions and consider children's circumstances under the totality framework. The rule requires every written USCIS denial to reflect consideration of each factor and specific articulation of reasons to help prevent misuse of age as a basis for denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health as a factor
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant's health is a mandatory factor; DHS will consider reports of immigration medical examinations (Form I-693) documenting Class A or Class B medical conditions and vaccination compliance where examinations are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere presence of a disability or medical condition will not alone render an applicant inadmissible. DHS will generally defer to civil surgeon/panel physician findings unless the report is incomplete. Officers are not medical professionals and should rely on the medical report when considering health in the totality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of disabilities and chronic conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Disability alone will never be a sufficient basis to determine that a noncitizen is likely at any time to become a public charge; DHS will not treat disabilities as outcome-determinative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some disabilities do not impact health or require extensive care. DHS will consider disabilities only to the extent they appear on the report of medical examination (Class A/B) and will provide further guidance to officers on how to assess whether a reported disability affects likelihood of becoming a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of medical examination reports (Form I-693) and Class A/B criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider any report of an immigration medical examination where required, which includes notation of Class A (e.g., drug abuse/addiction; conditions posing safety/welfare concerns) and Class B conditions (serious/permanent conditions that may interfere with self-care, work, or require extensive treatment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports include the nature/extent/remediability of abnormalities and the likelihood of requiring extensive medical care or institutionalization. DHS relies on designated physicians' findings to inform the health factor, except when the report appears incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drug abuse/addiction as health evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of drug abuse or addiction identified on a required immigration medical examination is part of the health factor that DHS will consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conditions are captured as Class A medical conditions on the medical report and will be weighed in the totality of circumstances. DHS declined to designate drug abuse or addiction categorically as a heavily weighted negative factor applicable in all cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and limitation for long-term institutionalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-term institutionalization in the context of Medicaid is limited to 'institutional services under section 1905(a) of the Social Security Act' and does not include home- and community-based services (HCBS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule also allows DHS to consider evidence submitted by applicants that alleged long-term institutionalization violates federal law (e.g., ADA or Rehabilitation Act). This narrows the scope of institutionalization considered adverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: No preset heavy or minimal weighting of factors
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not adopt a rule that certain statutory factors are 'heavily weighted' negative (or positive) factors or that any factor (other than lack of required affidavit) should be given minimal weight in every case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight given to factors depends on case-specific facts. DHS declined commenters' requests to add heavily weighted factors (including for drug abuse/addiction) or to instruct officers to give minimal weight to health in every case because such fixed weights would undermine fair, fact-specific determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written decision articulation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Every written denial decision issued by USCIS should reflect consideration of each of the factors outlined in the rule and provide specific articulation of the reasons for the officer's determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement is intended to promote clear, fair, and consistent public charge determinations and to help prevent misunderstandings of nondiscrimination laws (e.g., age discrimination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of empirical analysis and DHS guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS guidance includes empirical analysis of how the statutory factors (except for the Affidavit of Support) may affect the likelihood of becoming primarily dependent on government support, based on best-available data; officers should consider the factors and empirical evidence as described in the guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS may periodically issue guidance to inform the totality assessment. The guidance and empirical evidence are intended to assist officers in weighing factors (for example, how duration/recency of cash assistance affects predictions) but do not replace individualized analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on considering health insurance and social determinants as automatically favorable
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule does not define 'health' to include an assessment of whether an applicant has health insurance, and DHS declines to treat social determinants of health as automatically positive factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While DHS will consider circumstances affecting health as reflected in medical reports, it will not give positive weight to social determinants across the board; each case remains fact-specific and these background factors will be weighed as appropriate in the totality.
